question: The passage establishes that the principal development described in its opening paragraph was caused mainly by the factor discussed in its final paragraph.
supporting_evidence: Visitors sometimes complain that textiles, manuscripts and watercolours are displayed in galleries so dim that their details are difficult to see. From the visitor’s perspective, the solution appears obvious: increase the lighting. Conservators resist because light does not merely reveal an object; it also changes it. Pigments may fade, paper may yellow and fibres may weaken as absorbed energy triggers chemical reactions. The damage is cumulative and, unlike dust on glass, cannot simply be cleaned away. || Technology has improved monitoring, but it has not removed the judgement involved. Digital models can estimate fading, yet different dyes respond differently and an object’s earlier exposure may be unknown. Nor is perfect preservation always the sole aim. A ceremonial banner kept permanently in storage retains its fabric but loses its public role. Conversely, displaying it until its colours vanish would destroy evidence embedded in the material itself. Museums must decide what degree of change is acceptable, who should benefit from access and whether replicas provide an honest substitute. Dimness, then, is not merely a technical inconvenience. It represents a negotiated limit: enough light for an encounter, but not so much that the encounter consumes the object. The visitor sees reduced illumination; the institution is attempting to distribute visibility across generations.

Trains moving rapidly between towns required timetables that employees and passengers could interpret consistently, while signalling errors made disagreement between clocks dangerous. || Standardisation enabled coordination, but it also changed everyday expectations. A departure listed for a precise minute encouraged passengers to treat lateness differently from a coach said to leave in the morning. Factory work and telegraph communication reinforced the same discipline. Historians sometimes describe this as society becoming ruled by the clock, although ordinary life retained multiple temporalities: agricultural tasks followed weather and daylight, domestic labour rarely fitted a timetable and local customs survived within standard hours. Once commercial and administrative systems were organised around a common standard, opting out became difficult. The history illustrates how infrastructure can turn one convention into apparent common sense. Standard time succeeded not because it was more naturally true than local noon, but because a connected society required clocks to disagree less.
